[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_998_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.2 Estimating a linear regression model › 15.2.1 Using the lm() function (pages 610)
roles: formal, worked_example | topics: using-r, linear-regression, estimation
teaches: Shows how to fit a simple linear regression in R with lm(formula, data), using danielle_grump as the outcome and danielle_sleep as the sole predictor.
scope: R-specific simple linear regression with an intercept and one predictor. The coefficient interpretation continues in the next excerpt. It does not teach multiple regression.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_999_v2
As we saw with aov() in Comparing several means (one-way ANOVA), the output of the lm() function is a fairly complicated object, with quite a lot of technical information buried under the hood. Because this technical information is used by other functions, it’s generally a good idea to create a variable that stores the results of your regression. With this in mind, to run my linear regression, the command I want to use is this:

regression_1 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood

)

Note that I used danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep as the formula: in the model that I’m trying to estimate, danielle_grump is the outcome variable, and danielle_sleep is the predictor variable. It’s always a good idea to remember which one is which! Anyway, what this does is create an “lm object” (i.e., a variable whose class is "lm") called regression_1. Let’s have a look at what happens when we print() it out:

print(regression_1)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) danielle_sleep 125.956 -8.937

[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1003_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.3 Multiple linear regression › 15.3.1 Doing it in R (pages 612)
roles: formal, worked_example | topics: multiple-regression, linear-regression, estimation
teaches: Fits a two-predictor regression in R with lm, explains the implicit intercept, prints coefficients for danielle_sleep and baby_sleep, and interprets their relative sizes in the grumpiness example.
scope: R-specific multiple linear regression using danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep. The coefficient comments apply to this fitted parenthood model. The mentioned 3D regression-plane visualization is in excerpt 1004.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1004_v2
Multiple regression in R is no different to simple regression: all we have to do is specify a more complicated formula when using the lm() function. For example, if we want to use both danielle_sleep and baby_sleep as predictors in our attempt to explain why I’m so grumpy, then the formula we need is this:

danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep

Notice that, just like last time, I haven’t explicitly included any reference to the intercept term in this formula; only the two predictor variables and the outcome. By default, the lm() function assumes that the model should include an intercept (though you can get rid of it if you want). In any case, I can create a new regression model – which I’ll call regression_2 – using the following command:

regression_2 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood

)

And just like last time, if we print() out this regression model we can see what the estimated regression coeﬀicients are:

print(regression_2)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) danielle_sleep baby_sleep 125.96557 -8.95025 0.01052

[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1019_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.5 Hypothesis tests for regression models › 15.5.3 Running the hypothesis tests in R (pages 620)
roles: worked_example | topics: linear-regression, regression-diagnostics, hypothesis-tests
teaches: Runs summary() on an R multiple-regression model with danielle_sleep and baby_sleep, displaying residuals, coefficients, t tests, R-squared, and the model F test.
scope: R-specific multiple linear regression with two predictors. The excerpt displays output; the line-by-line interpretation and model comparison are in the next excerpt. Do not use it as a simple-regression example.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1020_v2
To compute all of the quantities that we have talked about so far, all you need to do is ask for a summary() of your regression model. Since I’ve been using regression_2 as my example, let’s do that:

summary(regression_2)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max

-11.0345 -2.2198 -0.4016 2.6775 11.7496 Coefficients:

Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)

(Intercept) 125.96557 3.04095 41.423 <2e-16 *** danielle_sleep -8.95025 0.55346 -16.172 <2e-16 *** baby_sleep 0.01052 0.27106 0.039 0.969

--Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.354 on 97 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.8161, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8123 F-statistic: 215.2 on 2 and 97 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16

The output that this command produces is pretty dense, but we’ve already discussed everything of interest in it, so what I’ll do is go through it line by line. The first line reminds us of what the actual regression model is:

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

[exc_45ecdb7da7734b_279_v3] Learning Statistics with jamovi: A Tutorial for Beginners in Statistical Analysis — Correlation and linear regression › 12.4 Estimating a linear regression model › 12.4.1 Linear regression in jamovi (pages 287)
roles: worked_example | topics: linear-regression, jamovi | figures: fig_45ecdb7da7734b_2224_v3, fig_45ecdb7da7734b_2225_v3
teaches: Fits a simple linear regression in jamovi with dani.grump as outcome and dani.sleep as the sole predictor, yielding intercept 125.96, slope -8.94, and fitted line Y-hat=125.96-8.94X.
scope: Jamovi-specific implementation using parenthood.csv. This is simple linear regression with one predictor and an intercept. The fitted numbers belong to that dataset and should not be used as a multiple-regression example or a general behavioral relationship.
To run my linear regression, open up the ‘Regression’ – ‘Linear Regression’ analysis in jamovi, using the parenthood.csv data file. Then specify dani.grump as the ‘Dependent Variable’ and dani.sleep as the variable entered in the ‘Covariates’ box. This gives the

results shown in Figure 12.13, showing an intercept 𝑏̂0 = 125.96 and the slope 𝑏̂1 = −8.94. In other words, the best fitting regression line that I plotted in Figure 12.12 has this formula:

𝑌𝑖̂ = 125.96 + (−8.94𝑋𝑖)

Figure 12.13. A jamovi screenshot showing a simple linear regression analysis

[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1020_v2] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.5 Hypothesis tests for regression models › 15.5.3 Running the hypothesis tests in R › 620 (pages 621)
roles: formal, worked_example | topics: multiple-regression, linear-regression, regression-diagnostics, hypothesis-tests
teaches: Interprets the R summary for a two-predictor regression: residual quartiles, coefficient estimates and t tests, N-K-1 degrees of freedom, the model F test, R-squared, and evidence for dropping baby_sleep.
scope: Interpretation is tied to the multiple-regression output in excerpt 1019. Its residual-quartile check is described as quick and rough, not a full diagnostics procedure. The conclusion that regression_1 is preferable applies to this example, where baby_sleep p=.969 and R-squared=.816.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_dd1e65de648fb2_1019_v2
You can see why this is handy, since it was a little while back when we actually created the regression_2 model, and so it’s nice to be reminded of what it was we were doing. The next part provides a quick summary of the residuals (i.e., the 𝜖𝑖 values), which can be convenient as a quick and dirty check that the model is okay. Remember, we did assume that these residuals were normally distributed, with mean 0. In particular it’s worth quickly checking to see if the median is close to zero, and to see if the first quartile is about the same size as the third quartile. If they look badly off, there’s a good chance that the assumptions of regression are violated. These ones look pretty nice to me, so let’s move on to the interesting stuff. The next part of the R output looks at the coeﬀicients of the regression model. Each row in this table refers to one of the coeﬀicients in the regression model. The first row is the intercept term, and the later ones look at each of the predictors. The columns give you all of the relevant information. The first column is the actual estimate of 𝑏 (e.g., 125.96 for the intercept, and -8.9 for the danielle_sleep predictor). The second column is the standard error estimate 𝜎̂𝑏. The third column gives you the 𝑡-statistic, and it’s worth noticing that in this table 𝑡 = 𝑏/̂ SE(𝑏)̂ every time.

roles: formal | topics: bayesian-inference, anova, linear-regression, regression-diagnostics, hypothesis-tests
Scope not reviewed. Check the source's applicability before using it.
danielle_sleep baby_sleep danielle_grump day 1 7.59 10.18 56 1 2 7.91 11.66 60 2 3 5.14 7.92 82 3 4 7.71 9.61 55 4 5 6.68 9.75 67 5 6 5.99 5.04 72 6

Back in Linear regression I proposed a theory in which my grumpiness (danielle_grump) on any given day is related to the amount of sleep I got the night before (danielle_sleep), and possibly to the amount of sleep our baby got (baby_sleep), though probably not to the day on which we took the measurement. We tested this using a regression model. In order to estimate the regression model we used the lm() function, like so:

model <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + day + baby_sleep, data = parenthood

)

The hypothesis tests for each of the terms in the regression model were extracted using the summary() function:

summary(model)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + day + baby_sleep,

data = parenthood)

BLAH BLAH BLAH Residual standard error: 4.375 on 96 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.8163, Adjusted R-squared: 0.8105 F-statistic: 142.2 on 3 and 96 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16

When interpreting the results, each row in this table corresponds to one of the possible predictors. The (Intercept) term isn’t usually interesting, though it is highly significant. The important thing for our purposes is the fact that danielle_sleep is significant at 𝑝 < .001 and neither of the other variables are.

Full reviewed notes: You can see why this is handy, since it was a little while back when we actually created the regression_2 model, and so it’s nice to be reminded of what it was we were doing. The next part of the R output looks at the coeﬀicients of the regression model. Each row in this table refers to one of the coeﬀicients in the regression model. The first row is the intercept term, and the later ones look at each of the predictors. The columns give you all of the relevant information. The first column is the actual estimate of 𝑏 (e.g., 125.96 for the intercept, and -8.9 for the danielle_sleep predictor). The second column is the standard error estimate 𝜎̂𝑏. The third column gives you the 𝑡-statistic, and it’s worth noticing that in this table 𝑡 = 𝑏/̂ SE(𝑏)̂ every time.

Finally, the fourth column gives you the actual 𝑝 value for each of these tests.5 The only thing that the table itself doesn’t list is the degrees of freedom used in the 𝑡-test, which is always 𝑁 − 𝐾 − 1 and is listed immediately below, alongside the 𝐹-test and the 𝑅2 values which assess the performance of the model as a whole. So in this case, the model performs significantly better than you’d expect by chance (𝐹(2,97) = 215.2, 𝑝 < .001), which isn’t all that surprising: the 𝑅2 = .816 value indicates that the regression model accounts for 81.6% of the variability in the outcome measure. However, when we look back up at the 𝑡-tests for each of the individual coeﬀicients, we have pretty strong evidence that the baby_sleep variable has no significant effect; all the work is being done by the danielle_sleep variable. Taken together, these results suggest that regression_2 is actually the wrong model for the data: you’d probably be better off dropping the baby_sleep predictor entirely. In other words, the regression_1 model that we started with is the better model.

At this stage however, there’s really only two of them that you care about, and as it turns out you’ve seen them before:

• formula. A formula that specifies the regression model. regression_1 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood

title: Simple Linear Regression in R with lm(): Fitting and Interpreting
content:
# Fitting and Interpreting Simple Linear Regression in R with `lm()`

**Scope:** This note covers R-specific simple linear regression — one outcome, one predictor, with an intercept — using `lm()` and `summary()`, following the *Learning Statistics with R* parenthood example (`danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep`). The `summary()` layout is illustrated with the book's two-predictor output so every column can be explained; the fitted simple-regression numbers shown are from the one-predictor model. Multiple regression, model comparison, and full diagnostics are out of scope.

## 1. Fitting the model

`lm()` has many arguments, but only two matter here:

- **`formula`** — specifies the model. For simple linear regression (one predictor plus an intercept) it takes the form `outcome ~ predictor`.
- **`data`** — the data frame containing the variables.

`lm()` returns a complicated object with technical information buried under the hood, and other functions use that information, so store the result in a variable:

```r
regression_1 <- lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)
```

- The formula `outcome ~ predictor` puts the **outcome** (`danielle_grump`) on the left and the **predictor** (`danielle_sleep`) on the right — always remember which is which.
- The intercept is included **by default**; you never type it into the formula.
- The result is an "lm object" (class `"lm"`).

## 2. Quick look: `print()`

```r
print(regression_1)
```

```
Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)  danielle_sleep
    125.956          -8.937
```

The `Call:` line reminds you what model you fitted. The coefficients give the best-fitting regression line:

$$\hat{Y_i} = -8.94\,X_i + 125.96$$

i.e. intercept $\hat{b}_0 = 125.96$ and slope $\hat{b}_1 = -8.94$.

## 3. Full output: `summary()`

`summary()` on a fitted model produces the dense output you actually interpret. Its structure (illustrated here with the book's two-predictor model, `regression_2`, so every section appears):

```
Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep + baby_sleep, data = parenthood)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max
-11.0345  -2.2198  -0.4016   2.6775   11.7496

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   125.96557    3.04095  41.423  <2e-16 ***
danielle_sleep -8.95025    0.55346 -16.172  <2e-16 ***
baby_sleep      0.01052    0.27106   0.039    0.969
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 4.354 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared: 0.8161,  Adjusted R-squared: 0.8123
F-statistic: 215.2 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
```

## 4. Reading the output, section by section

**Residuals.** A quick-and-dirty check that the model is okay. The model assumes residuals are normally distributed with mean 0, so check that the **median is close to 0** and the **1st and 3rd quartiles are about the same size**. If they look badly off, the regression assumptions are probably violated. (This is a rough check, not full diagnostics.)

**Coefficients table.** One row per coefficient: the intercept first, then each predictor. Four columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Estimate` | the coefficient estimate $\hat{b}$ (e.g. 125.96 for the intercept, −8.9 for the sleep predictor) |
| `Std. Error` | the standard error of the estimate, $\widehat{SE}(b)$ |
| `t value` | the t-statistic; note $t = \hat{b}\,/\,\widehat{SE}(b)$ every time |
| `Pr(>|t|)` | the p-value for the test of that coefficient |

The t-test degrees of freedom are not shown in the table; they are always $N - K - 1$ (sample size minus predictors minus 1) and appear just below. The `***` stars are significance codes (0 `***`, 0.001 `**`, 0.01 `*`, 0.05 `.`, 0.1 blank).

**Model-level statistics** (below the table):

- **Residual standard error** with its degrees of freedom — typical size of prediction error.
- **Multiple R-squared** — the proportion of variability in the outcome the model accounts for (e.g. $R^2 = .816$ means 81.6% of the variability is explained).
- **F-statistic** — tests whether the model as a whole performs better than chance (e.g. $F(2, 97) = 215.2$, $p < .001$).

## 5. Interpreting the example

- The slope of −8.94 means grumpiness drops as sleep increases; the intercept 125.96 is the fitted value at zero sleep (often not substantively interesting on its own).
- A significant F-test plus a large $R^2$ says the model works overall; the per-coefficient t-tests say *which* predictors are doing the work. In the book's two-predictor run, `baby_sleep` had $p = .969$ (no effect) while `danielle_sleep` did all the work — evidence that the simpler one-predictor model (`regression_1`) was the better model for those data.

## Key takeaways

1. Store the fit: `model <- lm(outcome ~ predictor, data = df)`.
2. `print(model)` for the fitted line; `summary(model)` for tests and fit statistics.
3. Check residual quartiles for a rough assumption check.
4. Read coefficients as estimate / SE / t (= estimate ÷ SE) / p-value, with df $= N - K - 1$.
5. Use $R^2$ and the F-test for the model as a whole; use the t-tests for individual predictors.

The study note is ready: **Simple Linear Regression in R with lm(): Fitting and Interpreting** (one note, ~1,300 tokens).

It covers, in order:
- **Fitting** — the two `lm()` arguments that matter (`formula`, `data`), the `outcome ~ predictor` syntax, the implicit intercept, and why to store the result in a variable.
- **Quick output** — `print()` on the one-predictor parenthood model, giving the fitted line Ŷ = −8.94X + 125.96.
- **Full output** — the `summary()` structure, illustrated with the book's two-predictor output so every section (residuals, coefficients table, model statistics) appears.
- **Line-by-line interpretation** — the residual-quartile sanity check, the four coefficient columns (Estimate, Std. Error, t = estimate ÷ SE, p-value) with df = N − K − 1, significance stars, residual standard error, R², and the model F-test.
- **Interpretation of the example** — what the slope and intercept mean, and how the F-test/R² (model as a whole) differ from the per-predictor t-tests.

The note is built from *Learning Statistics with R* (chapter 15, sections 15.2 and 15.5.3). One scope note: the book's `summary()` walkthrough uses its two-predictor model, so the note flags that the summary layout is shown from that output while the fitted simple-regression numbers come from the one-predictor model — multiple regression, model comparison, and full diagnostics are explicitly marked out of scope.
